title: US mail trains snatched mailbags from trackside posts without stopping

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still from 1903: a mailbag hangs from the arm of a white trackside post while a steam train approaches in the distance.

body: From the 1860s, many American passenger trains carried a **railway post office**: a car where clerks sorted letters while the train was moving. At small towns where the train did not stop, a local postal worker hung a pouch of outgoing mail on a trackside crane. As the train passed, often at 70 mph or more, a clerk swung out a hooked catcher arm that snagged the pouch, and at the same moment kicked a pouch of mail for the town out of the door.

slides.alt: Black-and-white film: a mailbag hangs from a white trackside post as a steam locomotive approaches and passes close by; as the last car goes past, the bag is gone and the empty arm springs up.
slides.caption: 1903: a steam train passes a mail crane. As the last car goes by, the bag is snatched away and the crane’s empty arm springs up.

slides.label: train routes with a railway post office at their height
slides.text: Together they covered more than 200,000 route miles in North America, and as many as a dozen clerks could work in one car.

slides.question: Clerks sat regular sorting tests. What accuracy score could still earn a clerk a warning?
slides.explanation: 96%. Clerks had to know every post office, junction and connection on their route, and the Railway Mail Service expected near-perfect sorting.
